facts.fact_text: On 9 September 2002, the applicant applied to the Chekhov Town Council for permission to hold a service in public.
The applicant requested permission to hold the public service between 11 a.m. and 1 p.m. on 22 or 29 September 2002.
On 20 September 2002, the deputy head of the Chekhov Town Council refused the applicant's request for permission to hold a public service.

The deputy head of the Chekhov Town Council stated that the Chekhov Town Council had on many occasions informed the applicant that it was not possible to hold services in public areas in the town (squares, streets, parks, etc.).

The Freedom of Conscience and Religious Associations Act (no. 125-FZ of 26 September 1997) provided that services and other religious rites and ceremonies in public were to be performed in accordance with the procedure established for assemblies, marches and demonstrations (section 16 of the Act).

The Decree of the Presidium of the USSR Supreme Council no. 9306-XI of 28 July 1988 provided that organisers of an assembly were to serve written notice on the municipal authorities no later than ten days before the planned assembly (section 2 of the Decree).

The Decree of the Presidium of the USSR Supreme Council no. 9306-XI of 28 July 1988 provided that the municipal authority was to give its response no later than five days before the planned assembly (section 3 of the Decree).

The Decree of the Presidium of the USSR Supreme Council no. 9306-XI of 28 July 1988 provided that an assembly could be banned if its purpose was contrary to the Constitution or threatened public order or the security of citizens.

The Chekhov Town Court of the Moscow Region ruled that a service of worship in a public area held by one religious organisation may lead to discontent of individuals of other denominations and public disorder.
